events.title: Can robots replace teachers?
events.speaker: Kavita Kapoor
events.speakerBio:
Kavita Kapoor is an award-winning technologist who collaborates with key decision-makers to create Technology for Good with a focus on child rights, volunteering and education. Her current portfolio covers, Founding Member and Strategy Director of the Federation of Humanitarian Technologists, Chief Learning Officer for the think tank Open UK, Trustee of South East River Trust, Founder of a grassroots LGBTQ+ sports club and mentor at the WISE Edinburgh Centre for Robotics.

Kavita trained as a coder and software architect for organisations as diverse as the BBC, Channel 4 Television and ICL Fujitsu and product manager with London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Going on to lead organisations globally she has held positions as CEO of What'sMySize, Regional Digital Operational Director working in Singapore and India and COO of the Micro:bit Educational Foundation.

Her awards includes a BAFTA for Channel 4, Luvvies for London 2012 and MIT IIC for the BBC micro:bit.
events.description:
Welcome to this first meeting of the new Data Science in Education group! We have founded this group to be a home for data scientists working in the EdTech space, because within general data science and machine learning groups education has a very small voice.

For this inaugural meeting we are very fortunate to have Kavita Kapoor as our speaker. This meeting will also be an opportunity to find out more about the group and influence the direction.

“Can robots replace teachers? AI in education - the case for creativity”
Learn how machine learning and AI are both teaching through automated adaptive learning but also encroaching on children’s and teachers’ human rights. Kavita in conjunction with the Women Leading in AI - Education working group, present research on how this sector has been evolving across the world. Some countries are focused on teaching ethical data skills and others are focused on getting young people through university entrance exams, still others are focused on creating cyber speciali

events.title: Using unconventional data sets to understand what's going on in education
events.speaker: Timo Hannay
events.speakerBio: Timo Hannay is the founder of SchoolDash (https://www.schooldash.com/), an education data analytics firm that works with a wide range of collaborators, including media, publishers, edtech, charities, trusts and government. He is also a non-executive director of SAGE Publishing and of Arden University, and an advisor to Ada Lovelace Day and Maths4Girls. He was previously the founding managing director of Digital Science and before that variously ran the online business of Nature Publishing Group, worked as a consultant at McKinsey & Company, wrote for The Economist, and investigated brain physiology at the University of Oxford and Waseda University in Tokyo.
events.description: The Covid-19 pandemic has disrupted not only education, but also the collection of data about education, with exams cancelled, inspections postponed and information-gathering processes inside schools hugely disrupted. Together with collaborators from across education, edtech and government, SchoolDash has been using unconventional data sources – from formative assessment tests and wellbeing surveys to application usage logs and school websites – to gather information about the effects of school closures and make it available to education leaders and policymakers in near real time. This experience also points towards better ways to analyse and understand education in the post-pandemic world.

events.title: Advances and Opportunities: Data Science for Education
events.speaker: Aigner Picou
events.speakerBio: Aigner, a Program Director at The Learning Agency Lab, will talk about recent Lab efforts to leverage data science for education by releasing new datasets and launching education-focused data science competitions.
events.description:
Crowdsourced solutions have been shown to kickstart new fields and develop new solutions. When the problem is narrowly defined — and has an algorithmic solution — data science competitions have yielded large results in areas ranging from home valuation to cervical cancer screening.

While these kinds of competitions are prominent in other fields, data science competitions in education remain substantially underleveraged. In the past 10 years, there have been few education data competitions that have attracted more than 500 teams.

There are signs of change, for sure. CommonLit ran a crowdsourced competition this past year that drew in over 3,000 participants! With the amount of data being produced by learning platforms and major advances in fields like natural language processing and machine learning, now is an opportune time to explore how data science can be used to improve education.

events.title: Describing Complex Things Simply: Visualising Survey Data for Schools
events.speaker: Janis Strods and Iona Kelliher
events.speakerBio:
Janis is one of the founders and the Chief Product Officer of Edurio, a survey tool for schools and multi-academy trusts, and is working to make sure data visualisation leads to school improvement. Previously he's published research on agent-based models of human behaviour.
Iona is Edurio's Head of Research and oversees the development of new surveys and the analysis of survey data. She is responsible for the evolution of our reporting process and outputs, and the development of insight-led thought leadership.
events.description: Janis and Iona work on data visualisation for Edurio — an edTech startup helping schools and multi-academy trusts understand stakeholder feedback. In this session Janis will share Edurio's journey of creating interactive online reports for their users, trying to make the complex multi-level data accessible without oversimplifying it. Iona will then delve deeper in our thought leadership work, and the challenges around translating a huge and interesting dataset into a digestible static report. Edurio's reports are available at home.edurio.com/insights

events.title: Improving Argumentation Skill Learning Through Artificial Intelligence
events.speaker: Thiemo Wambsganss
events.speakerBio: Thiemo Wambsganss is a research associate at the Institute of Information Systems at the University of St. Gallen (Switzerland), advised by Prof. Dr. Jan Marco Leimeister. Moreover, since April 2021 Thiemo is a Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) fellow and a research collaborator at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University, where he is collaborating with Ken Koedinger on adaptive argumentation.
events.description:
Abstract
Argumentation is an omnipresent rudiment of daily communication and thinking. The ability to form convincing arguments is not only fundamental to persuading an audience of novel ideas but also plays a major role in strategic decision-making, negotiation, and constructive civil discourse. However, humans often struggle to develop argumentation skills owing to a lack of individual and instant feedback in their learning process, since providing feedback on the individual argumentation skills of learners is time-consuming and not scalable if conducted manually by educators. Building on self-regulated learning theory, I follow a design oriented research approach to investigate a set of theory-based design principles for a novel class of AI-based argumentation tutoring systems. The proposed systems provide learners with adaptive self-evaluation opportunities based on logical argumentation errors irrespective of instructor, time, and location. To evaluate the principles’ feasibility, I instantiate, develop, demonstrate, and evaluate three AI-based argumentation tutoring systems. I evaluated the novel artifact class in comparison to traditional argumentation learning systems across three empirical studies. As these technologies advance further, I hope my work will support researchers in Natural Language Processing, Human-Computer Interaction and Educational Technology when designing new AI-based skill learning systems to leverage these systems’ full potential for a metacognition skill-based future (continuous) education.

events.title: Live remote instruction in the primary phase: experiences of teachers & parents
events.speaker: Becky Allen
events.speakerBio:
Becky Allen is Chief Analyst and a co-founder of Teacher Tapp, the largest teacher survey and professional development tool in the UK. She is also a Professor of Education at the University of Brighton. Until 2018, she was Professor of Education at UCL Institute of Education and over her academic career she has written extensively on school accountability, admissions, assessment, expenditure and teacher careers.

An economist by training and former secondary school teacher, she is an expert in the analysis of large datasets. Between 2014 and 2017, she was the founding Director of Education Datalab, a non-profit research organisation that has developed a reputation for making complex, quantitative analysis accessible for those involved with running schools. In 2018, she chaired a government working group to review how data is used in schools. Her book on teacher careers called ‘The Teacher Gap’ was published in 2018 and her new book ‘The Next Big Thing in School Improvement’ was published in 2021.
events.description:
During the 2021 Spring lockdown, around half of primary schools offered daily live instruction to children at home. Teacher Tapp monitored the experiences of parents and teachers via daily survey questions.

In this talk, Becky will describe the challenges of surveying parents and teachers, dealing with missing data and creating overall measures of learning experiences and wellbeing. She will show how the experience of live instruction affected parental perceptions of time spent learning, their child’s motivation and their own well-being.

events.title: Building the Standard for Skills-Based Recruitment
events.speaker: Sofiane Bébert and Alex Alexandrescu
events.speakerBio:
Sofiane (Co-Founder & CTO @ Dicey Tech)
Born and raised in Niger, Sofiane came to the University of Manchester in 2011 to study an MEng in Mechatronic Engineering.

Growing up in a family environment that emphasised education and the transformative impact it has on people's lives, he always had a passion for technology and especially in education.

Alex (Co-Founder & CEO @ Dicey Tech)
Alex is a Romanian-born and Manchester-bred entrepreneur. With a background in strategy consulting, he rediscovered a childhood passion for technology and digital making when he assembled his first 3D printer. This led to a 3 month period where he learned how to design and code, sparked by the curiosity and desire to build his own toys.
events.description:
**Please note: To book tickets for this event you need to register on eventbrite:**

https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/building-the-standard-for-skills-based-recruitment-tickets-522637100637

Dicey Tech is an EdTech company that is focused on helping companies surface and nurture emerging talent.

The fundamental problem that they’ve been obsessing with for the past 5 years is that industry is evolving faster than education. By the time new knowledge makes its way into mainstream education, that knowledge likely becomes obsolete. Since innovation is driven by industry, they believe that a core aspect of solving this problem is for companies to get involved and help create the content that educates young people.

But there’s another aspect, which is much more fundamental to solving the problem of a lagging educational system. Since the role of education is to feed into employment, the key to fundamentally unlocking innovation in education is to change how we recruit.

Alex & Sofiane will talk about the challenges that Dicey Tech faced, including working with schools during the pandemic and building products in the challenging EdTech space. We will also hear about how they were able to pivot their business to a skills platform.

events.title: Using intelligent social agents in informal learning
events.speaker: Bethanie Maples
events.speakerBio:
Bethanie is the Technology Lead at X, the moonshot factory, where she designs embodied artificial intelligence and human-machine interface platforms and systems. She is focused on cognitive development and education and her technical skills cover learning design, natural language processing, machine learning, conversational agents, human-in-the-loop systems, social cognition and affective neuroscience, and machine tutors.

Her first book chapter was published earlier this year in [AI in Learning: Designing the Future](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-09687-7). This covered the use of generative AI for education - the future of personal AI agents likes Replika (which uses GPT3 and its own generative language models), and designing them to help us learn.
events.description:
Intelligent social agents are designed to interact in human-like ways and have recently received significant attention due to the popularity of ChatGPT. This has lead many people to ask where they might fit within education, with strong opinions on either side.

Our speaker this month is as expert in intelligent social agents, and will be helping us understand their potential to support learning that takes place outside of the traditional classroom setting.

Overall, this talk will be of interest to anyone interested in the intersection of technology and learning, as well as those seeking to understand how intelligent social agents can be leveraged to enhance informal learning experiences.

events.title: Education in the Wake of the Covid-19 Pandemic: What the data say
events.speaker: Timo Hannay
events.speakerBio: Timo Hannay is the founder of [SchoolDash](https://www.schooldash.com/), an education data analytics firm that works with a wide range of clients and collaborators, including media organisations, publishers, edtech companies, charities, school trusts and government departments. He is also a non-executive director of SAGE Publishing, EDUCATE Ventures and Arden University, and an advisor to Ada Lovelace Day, Maths4Girls and The Great Imagining.  He was previously the founding managing director of Digital Science and before that variously ran the online business of Nature Publishing Group, worked as a consultant at McKinsey & Company, wrote for The Economist, and investigated brain physiology at the University of Oxford and Waseda University in Tokyo.
events.description: For three years, the British education system, like other parts of our society and economy, has been through a profound disruption caused by the Covid-19 pandemic and associated lockdowns. What effect has this had on schools, educators and above all on children themselves? This talk will review a wide range of data from official and unofficial sources to assess the state of England's schools and their pupils, and try to anticipate where things might go next.

events.title: Using Augmented Reality games to help children fall in love with mathematics
events.speaker: Grace Olugbodi
events.speakerBio:
Grace Olugbodi is the creator of the multi-award-winning maths board game Race To Infinity and author of the book "Make Maths Fun". Grace's mission is to help 10 million children love maths and eliminate Maths Anxiety by creating products that reduce anxiety, make maths fun, increase confidence, and improve children's life chances.

The Race To Infinity game is available in 12 countries and has won numerous national and international awards, including endorsements from National Numeracy, Tower Hamlets Education BP, and the Good Toy Guide. Additionally, Grace serves as the chair of governors in a primary school and director of trustees in a Multi-Academy Trust (MAT). She has spoken at Barclays Plc, the London School of Economics, Department of International Trade, and the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO). Grace was awarded an Honorary Doctorate Degree from London Metropolitan University in recognition of her work in helping children fall in love with Maths.
events.description:
We create maths games for kids to help them love maths, increase confidence and eliminate mathematical anxiety.

We started with physical board games and are now digitising our proven, flagship game.

Our software unleashes the power of data to automate helping kids learn maths through games, thereby increasing confidence and reducing maths anxiety. We eliminate hours offrustration for kids, parents and teachers by fast tracking progress.

events.title: What does it mean for an Edtech company to be data driven?
events.speaker: Francisco Díaz
events.speakerBio: We are delighted to welcome Sumdog's Lead Data Analyst as our speaker for this event. With a background in biomedical engineering, he is passionate about using data and mathematical models to explore and understand the world and its workings. In his current role as Lead Data Analyst for Sumdog, he has the exciting task of leveraging data from millions of students across the world to help provide accessible and personalised education and bridge the educational gap.
events.description: The last decade has seen an increasing trend of companies defining themselves as 'data-driven'. However, it is a buzzword often used ambiguously or with a vague reference about what aspects are impacted by data. We will explore, from the perspective of an educational technology business, how data is embedded within day-to-day operations. From discussing what areas of a company can be improved through the use of data (hint: almost all of them) to reviewing the various agents that benefit from data-driven insights, we will examine how data can be used to help close the attainment gap within the educational system.

events.title: LLMs for Formative Assessment: Pre-training vs fine-tuning vs prompt-engineering
events.speaker: Owen Henkel
events.speakerBio:
Owen Henkel is currently a graduate researcher at the University of Oxford, where his research focuses on applying advanced NLP methods to aid both the teaching and formative assessment of foundational literacy and numeracy skills. He also leads the AI and Data Science teams at Rising Academies, and education company building Rori an AI-powered chatbot that provides personalized math tutoring, on low-cost mobile phones.

Before Oxford, he founded and worked as Investment Director at Pearson Ventures, a 50M early-stage investment fund, where he led new investments and served as a board member on multiple portfolio companies. Previously, Owen was Director of Research and Efficacy, at Pearson Affordable Learning Fund, which invested in education entrepreneurs operating in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and Latin America.

Earlier in his career, he was a consultant at McKinsey and Co., completed a dual MBA/MA at the University of Michigan, and taught in New Orleans as part of Teach for America.
events.description:
The rapid progress in LLMs has been an exciting development in the field of AIED, and this talk discusses potential applications of LLMs to support formative assessment, specifically of literacy. Prior to the emergence of the most recent generation of LLMs (e.g., GPT 4, Bard, Claude), there had been promising research pointing to the potential for fine-tuned LLMs to assist with formative assessment. However, these results depended on fine-tuning models, which requires significant technical expertise and the resource-intensive process of collecting and labeling large data sets. Furthermore, such fine-tuned models often struggle to generalize to similar but distinct tasks, for instance, reading comprehension in a different topic or level of difficulty. The newer generation of LLM models (those that have been trained using RLHF or similar methods) have many additional capabilities, and with careful prompt design and few-shot learning, may also be well-suited to evaluate student responses to reading comprehension questions.

This talk will include a recap of recent advances in NLP, discuss different paradigms for customizing LLMs to evaluate student work, and will present recent empirical research on using LLMs to mark formative reading ability assessments.

events.title: OATutor: An Open-source Adaptive Tutoring System and Curated Content Library
events.speaker: Zachary Pardos
events.speakerBio:
[Dr. Pardos](https://bse.berkeley.edu/zachary-pardos) is an Associate Professor of Education at UC Berkeley studying adaptive learning and AI. His early scholarship focused on formative assessment using Knowledge Tracing, the predominant model used for estimating skill mastery in computer tutoring system contexts. His recent work designing Human-AI collaborations to pave pathways to and within systems of higher education has been published in venues such as SIGCHI, AAAI, The Internet and Higher Education, PLoS ONE, and Science. This work has included the development of high-quality tools used by tens of thousands of users, including course recommender systems ([AskOski.com](http://askoski.com/)), a python library for knowledge tracing ([pyBKT.com](http://pybkt.com/)), and an open-source adaptive tutoring system and creative commons content library ([OATutor.io](http://oatutor.io/)).

He earned his PhD in Computer Science at Worcester Polytechnic Institute with a dissertation on computational models of cognitive mastery estimation. Funded by a National Fellowship, he spent extensive time with K-12 educators and students working to integrate educational technology into the curriculum as a formative assessment tool. After completing his PhD in 2012, he spent one year as a Postdoctoral Associate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. At UC Berkeley, he directs the Computational Approaches to Human Learning (CAHL) Research Lab, teaches in the Data Science undergraduate program, and is an affiliated faculty in Cognitive Science.
events.description: Despite decades long establishment of effective tutoring principles, no adaptive tutoring system has been developed and open-sourced to the research community. The absence of such a system inhibits researchers from replicating adaptive learning studies and extending and experimenting with various tutoring system design directions. For this reason, adaptive learning research is primarily conducted on a small number of proprietary platforms. In the work presented here, we aimed to democratize adaptive learning research with the introduction of the first open-source adaptive tutoring system based on Intelligent Tutoring System principles. The system, we call Open Adaptive Tutor (OATutor), has been iteratively developed over three years with field trials in classrooms drawing feedback from students, teachers, and researchers. The MIT-licensed source code includes three creative commons (CC BY) textbooks worth of algebra problems, with tutoring supports authored by the OATutor project. Future avenues and early ChatGPT-based experiment results using OATutor will be discussed.

events.title: Charting Success: Using Data to Guide Product Migration in EdTech
events.speaker: Elanor King
events.speakerBio:
Irish native Elanor King is currently the Data Engineering Manager at Sparx Learning, a platform that provides maths and reading homework solutions to nearly half the schools in the country. Elanor was employee #7 in HegartyMaths, so has tried her hand at most functions while the business was growing, from Product Owner, Customer Services Manager to Data Lead.

Her professional journey boasts diverse milestones. Prior to her current role, she led a team implementing a collection of scientific publishing sites and spent some years developing cryptographic libraries in C++. There has also been a touch of teaching and, of all things, knitwear design along the way.

Elanor's path showcases a fusion of technology, education, and creativity that has shaped her into the multifaceted professional she is today.
events.description:
In the dynamic landscape of educational technology, the strategic merger of two key players, Sparx Learning and HegartyMaths, marks a defining moment for the future of homework. This presentation celebrates the strengths of Sparx Maths, the legacy of HegartyMaths and unveils the pivotal role data played in orchestrating a successful product migration.

As per the best-loved homework instructions, we will “compare and contrast” the two product offerings, and the culture of use surrounding them. We will explain (with charts!) the key data that helped our teachers transfer their trust from one beloved platform to another and why this will help more students to master more maths.

This talk will take you through the highs and lows of merging the tech and data of two EdTech pioneers, shows off our data-driven success, and points to an exciting future for the learning of our students.

events.title: AI for Teacher Development: exploring future possibilities
events.speaker: David Weston
events.speakerBio: David Weston is the founder and Co-Chief Executive of the Teacher Development Trust, the national charity for effective professional development in schools and colleges. He founded the Trust in 2012 after spending ten years as a secondary school maths and physics teacher and experiencing a growing frustration with the way that teachers are developed across the school system. Since its launch, David has steered the Trust to be one of the foremost voices in education on the subject of professional development. From March 2015 he was the Chair of the Department for Education’s Teachers’ Professional Development Expert Group for England. Alongside co-author Bridget Clay, David wrote Unleashing Great Teaching: the secrets to the most effective teacher development and co-authored a review on evidence around teacher working conditions. A former software engineer, he has been leading discussions and experiments in using Artificial Intelligence to improve teacher development. He has written extensively in the TES, Guardian, Schools Week and a number of other education journals and newspapers and speaks frequently on teacher development and school leadership. He has had a number of radio and TV appearances speaking about teaching, teacher development and LGBT issues. David works closely with stakeholders across the sector including government ministers and policy-makers and helped to set up the Chartered College of Teaching – of which he is now a Founding Fellow. He is a trustee of the Teaching Awards Trust and an advocate for LGBT teachers and founded OutTeacher, which has become LGBTed.
events.description: In this talk, David Weston will review some of the latest applications of AI to support the development of teachers, whether initial training, continuing development or developing coaches and leaders. This will include feedback tools on transcripts and video, simulations, reflection tools and more. David will also reflect on some of the research on teacher expertise and how to align tools so that it supports and develops this, rather than working in a way that diminishes it or risks teacher morale and retention.

events.title: Beyond Right or Wrong: Leveraging LLMs to Enhance the Learning Process
events.speaker: Rose E Wang
events.speakerBio: Rose E. Wang is a fourth year Computer Science PhD student at Stanford University, advised by Dorottya (Dora) Demszky. She works on natural language processing (NLP) and education, and is gratefully funded by the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship and the National Student Support Accelerator. She completed her undergraduate studies at MIT, where she worked with Professor Joshua Tenenbaum, Professor Jonathan How, the Google Brain team (student researcher) and Google Brain Robotics team (internship). She has received several awards for her research, including best paper award in computational modeling at CogSci 2020, best paper award at NeurIPS 2020 Cooperative AI workshop, and an oral presentation at ICLR 2022 (<1.6%).
events.description:
Recent advances in natural language processing have stirred excitement about large language models (LLMs) used to provide equitable access to high-quality education. Current education paradigms have a strong focus on the learning outcome—e.g., whether the student gets their answer correct. My research challenges those paradigms by leveraging LLMs to focus on the process—e.g., how are students arriving at their answer? I’m interested in using LLMs to understand and support both how teachers teach and how students learn.

In this talk, I will focus on understanding and supporting teachers’ remediation process, i.e., how teachers respond to student mistakes. I will discuss one recent submission which explores the potential of LLMs to assist math tutors in remediating student mistakes. Our work presents ReMath, a benchmark co-developed with experienced math teachers, which provides a comprehensive deconstruction of their thought process for effective remediation. This benchmark encompasses three crucial tasks: (1) inferring the type of student error, (2) determining the appropriate strategy and intention to address the error, and (3) generating a response that incorporates this information. We evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art instruct-tuned and dialog models on ReMath. Our findings suggest that although models consistently improve upon original tutor responses, we cannot rely on models alone to remediate mistakes. Providing models with the error type (e.g., the student is guessing) and strategy (e.g., simplify the problem) leads to a 75% improvement in the response quality over models without that information. Nonetheless, despite the improvement, the quality of the best model’s responses still falls short of experienced math teachers. Our work sheds light on the potential and current limitations of using LLMs to provide high-quality learning experiences for both tutors and students at scale.

events.title: Conceptualizing and Measuring Engagement in Digital Learning Platforms
events.speaker: Caitlin Mills
events.speakerBio: Caitlin Mills is an Assistant Professor of Educational Psychology and Co-Director of the Learning Informatics Lab at the University of Minnesota. Before joining Minnesota, she spent four years in the Psychology Department at the University of New Hampshire. She is interested in the intersection of cognitive psychology, computer science, and education. Most of her research has focused on the antecedents and consequences of mind wandering, the influence of affective states on information processing, and engagement/disengagement during complex learning.
events.description: According to most theories, engagement is considered a necessary part of learning. For digital learning platforms, this can be particularly important to consider given that their effectiveness may be highly dependent on the ability to maintain student engagement both in the moment and over time. At the same time, it can often be difficult to assess whether a student is engaged vs. disengaged, especially at times when they experience what is commonly known as "zoning out" or when their thoughts wander off to different topics. In this talk, I will discuss a few different ways that engagement can be conceptualized across different learning platforms, followed by some recent examples of how machine learning can be used to make real-time predictions about engagement in order to deliver interventions that offer "in the moment" support to improve learning outcomes.

events.title: Integrated procedural and neural computing as a software engineering problem
events.speaker: Theodore Gray
events.speakerBio: Theodore Gray is a co-founder of Wolfram Research and inventor of the Notebook user interface paradigm. He is a NYT Best-selling author for The Elements and BAFTA award winner for Disney Animated. Recently he returned to Wolfram Research as Director of Education Technology concentrating on an AI-based tutoring system.
events.description: AIs, like humans, often need to operate in structured environments in which they interface with rigid, procedural systems. A customer service rep, whether human or AI, needs to match vaguely-specified human desires with the particular actions the company allows. Similarly, a teacher or tutor, whether human or AI, needs to have flexible, adaptive conversations with a student, but at the same time guide them through a pre-specified curriculum sequence and prepare them for a very specific set of tests and external assessments. The tutor needs to record student progress and grades in a rigid learning management system, maintain long-term memory of the students existing knowledge, and so on. We have been working on tools to facilitate the creation, testing, and debugging of such hybrid LLM/procedural interactions, approaching the situation as a software engineering problem that requires an IDE (Integrated Development Environment), debugging tools, and regression testing tools.

events.title: Can edtech study its impact in schools?
events.speaker: John F. Brown
events.speakerBio: Dr John F. Brown is a director of What Worked Education and statistician at Durham University and the Education Endowment Foundation involved in meta analysis. Formerly a senior researcher for DfE and Academy Trusts in London.
events.description: Much edtech reaches children through schools, indicating that what goes on in schools, is likely to greatly influence edtechs impact on outcomes. If we want to know how effective edtech is at improving outcomes it is arguably necessary to study their effectiveness including the influence of schools. However, schools are not the easiest places to arrange impact studies because their bandwidth is often consumed with their primary objectives of safety, administration of activities, behaviour and teaching. This talk suggests edtech should not be put off from attempting to do studies with schools because the difficulties are only skin deep. Overcoming initial barriers shows schools are almost ideally organised/structured to carry out high quality education research with hardly any inconvenience to themselves. This is because schools are organised into groups of comparable children, classes, that are selected on a scale of ability in a subject (setting). Meaning, the subject departments have ready made groups of similar children, so if edtech is given to one class and not the other any difference in outcome is likely to only be the edtech. The talk sketches out other ways schools are set up to be nearly ideal for measuring the impact of edtech, advocating for school studies to be approached more enthusiastically.

events.title: Developing LearnLM-Tutor: An Evaluation-Driven Approach to GenAI for Education
events.speaker: Markus Kunesch
events.speakerBio: Markus is a Senior Research Engineer at Google DeepMind, where he is co-tech lead of the AI for Education programme. His work is focused on generative AI and AI ethics, with a particular interest in sociotechnical systems and translating social science research into new evaluations and modeling approaches. Before embarking on AI research, Markus completed a PhD in black hole physics.
events.description: Recent advances in generative AI have brought renewed interest in AI as a tool for teaching and learning. In this talk, I will present our work on improving the pedagogical capabilities of Gemini to build the LearnLM-Tutor. I will outline the whole modeling and development cycle, with a focus on our participatory approach to evaluating the model's pedagogical capabilities, and how we are translating learning science principles into educational benchmarks and fine-tuning datasets. The LearnLM-tutor is preferred over prompted Gemini by both educators and learners, but it is only a first step and I will describe the open challenges in training and evaluating generative AI for education.

events.title: Learning Error Representations for Student Modeling and Content Generation
events.speaker: Andrew Lan
events.speakerBio: Andrew Lan an assistant professor in the Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences, University of Massachusetts Amherst. Prior to that, he was a postdoctoral research associate at Princeton University and received his M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in Electrical and Computer Engineering in May 2014 and May 2016, respectively, from the Digital Signal Processing (DSP) group at Rice University. He was also affiliated with OpenStax. His research focuses on the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and especially natural language processing (NLP) methods to enable scalable and effective personalized learning in education, spanning areas such as learner modeling, personalization, content generation, and human-in-the-loop AI. His work has been recognized by awards including the NSF CAREER award, several best paper awards and nominations, and grand prizes at the NAEP Reading/Math Automated Scoring Challenges.
events.description: Classic work in student modeling, such as item response theory and knowledge tracing, do not consider the textual content of assessment questions, which results in limited model capacity and generalization across learning scenarios, preventing them from being applied to more open-ended interactions like dialogues. In this talk, we will discuss our work on taking the first steps toward powerful and generalizable, large language model (LLM)-based student models, along two directions: error representation learning in math multiple-choice questions and error mode tracking among students. We will detail two frameworks: DiVERT (Distractor Generation with Variational Errors Represented as Text) for math multiple-choice questions and OKT (open-ended knowledge tracing). Both will be key components of next-generation LLM-based student models and simulated student agents.

events.title: Not Perfect but Good Enough? Our Experience Using GPT as a Homework Agent
events.speaker: Sankalan Pal Chowdhury
events.speakerBio: Sankalan Pal Chowdhury is a second-year Ph.D. student at ETH Zurich whose work primarily focuses on improving the tutoring abilities of large language models.
events.description: Sankalan and his colleague Alessandro recently concluded a field trial of using ChatGPT to provide interactive English homework to students in an Italian High School. While observed learning gains were limited, students were quite excited about it, and most of them wanted to continue using it. Further, despite students having rather long conversations with GPT, there was very little hallucination observed(less than 1% of questions). While GPT is still far from perfect, the community needs to consider that are its issues strong enough to keep students from using it, even if the alternative is a complete lack of one-on-one tutoring.

events.title: Revealing Pathways to Earnings and Employment Through the LEO Dataset
events.speaker: Steve Preston and Joe Miller
events.speakerBio:
**Steve Preston – Managing Director, Mime** 
Steve has worked in the education sector since 2003 and founded Mime in 2007 to bring his innovative ideas to a wider audience. Steve is an experienced education researcher and has led several large research projects involving accessing secure government datasets. His expertise in all areas of education data coupled with his clarity of thought in solving complex problems makes him a thought leader in the education data field. His advice is regularly sought by the DfE, BEIS, GLA and the Cabinet Office as well as other charities and public bodies and he has spoken at conferences in the UK and abroad. 

Steve led Mime’s work with TASO, setting the overall approach and guiding the analysis throughout. Steve has authored a range of published research on the education pathways of young people in England, including a large GLA-funded project using NPD data to better understand the post-16 landscape in London. 

Steve is an ONS accredited researcher and has a first-class degree in Industrial Economics from Nottingham University. 
 
**Joe Miller – Senior Consultant, Mime** 
Joe has been involved in education data and policy since 2017. Having previously worked in the Wellcome Trust’s education team, he joined Mime in 2019, where he has led projects for a wide range of public sector organisations and education charities. Joe has built a strong understanding of the data on young people in England and regularly presents to both local and regional government. He is also often approached by senior education leaders for his insight and guidance. 
Joe carried out the analysis of the LEO dataset for Mime’s work with TASO and led the report write-up. He has also led previous projects using person-level secure government datasets. 

Joe is an ONS accredited researcher and studied Economics at Cambridge University, followed by an MSc in Public Policy at UCL.
events.description:
Transforming Access and Student Outcomes in Higher Education (TASO), the “what works?” institute for higher education, commissioned Mime to explore the impact of different post-16 pathways on long term outcomes.

We secured access to the Longitudinal Educational Outcomes (LEO) dataset to track more than a million young people through school, further education, higher education and into the labour market. The novel dataset produced revealed new insights about the impact of different educational pathways on future earnings and employment rates for different demographic groups. This groundbreaking research filled a significant evidence gap and resulted in several new findings with important implications for policy-makers and for individuals making decisions about their own education pathways.

In our presentation we will provide information on our method and learnings from working with LEO data, as well as explaining key findings from our research. This will include:

* What are the opportunities that LEO data has opened up for researchers, particularly when linked to other person-level datasets?
* What are some of the challenges and limitations when working with LEO data?
* What can we learn about post-16 pathways from the LEO dataset?

events.title: On the Promising Path of Making Education Effective for Every Student
events.speaker: Allen Nie
events.speakerBio: Allen Nie is a Ph.D. student in computer science at Stanford University, advised by Professor Emma Brunskill and Chris Piech. His research area includes offline reinforcement learning and causal inference with applications in education. He interned at Microsoft Research and Google DeepMind. His Ph.D. is supported by a Yee-Hoffman grant from the Stanford Human-Centered AI Institute (HAI). He has published papers in NeurIPS, ICLR, AAAI, ACL, EMNLP, MLJ, and education conferences such as LAK and AIED.
events.description: Traditional classroom teaching is an example of scaling education with a one-size-fits-all strategy, but modern machine learning algorithms are promised to adapt and personalize for each student. Can we succeed and what are the harms and benefits of introducing AI into the classroom? In this talk, I will discuss the future of using RL to advance education. I will show the real world result of how an RL system can offer personalized math tutoring to a group 2-4th grade students and what that personalization looks like. Then, with the rapid advancement in large language models, I will discuss a recent work where we directly put GPT-4 in the hands of 5831 students around the world, accompanied by a randomized control trial study. We show that while LLM holds the promise to provide data-efficient personalized tutoring for students, there is a mixed effect when introducing students to such a tool. Together, we show the promise of AI-enhanced education that can enable current and future generations to learn, achieve, and self-actualize. With more careful and pioneering research to come, the prospect of enhancing educational fairness and equity for every student is more promising than ever.

events.title: Plotting in LiveHintAI: Challenges, Solutions, and Opportunities
events.speaker: Thomas Christie
events.speakerBio: Thomas Christie leads the Engineering Hub for the Learning Engineering Virtual Institute. Formerly a math teacher, Thomas holds a PhD in Cognitive Science and has worked in educational technology for over a decade. He lives in St Paul, Minnesota with his family.
events.description: Carnegie Learning is developing LiveHintAI, a system designed to deliver contextually relevant, on-demand support to students learning mathematics. In middle school algebra, clarifying connections between algebraic relationships and their graphical representations on Cartesian coordinates is critical. This talk presents our collaborative work to enable LiveHintAI to dynamically generate Desmos plots during tutor-student dialogues. We’ll share some challenges we encountered and the techniques we used to overcome them.

events.title: Deeper Thinking Through Open Response: Using LLMs for Marking and Feedback
events.speaker: Jamie Conn and Matt Drew
events.speakerBio:
**Matt Drew**
Data Scientist in the Modelling & Research team at Sparx. Works largely on the monitoring, development, and deployment of the various models used in our products.

**Jamie Conn**
Leads the product development of Sparx Science. Formerly a Data Scientist developing personalisation algorithms used across Sparx products.
events.description:
Sparx Science is an online homework system used weekly by 400,000+ students in England, part of the broader Sparx portfolio which serves 2,600+ schools and 2.2m+ students.

Traditionally, open-response questions—requiring students to answer with anything from a few words to full paragraphs—have required marking by teachers. As a result, online homework systems typically relied on constrained question types, such as multiple-choice.
However, Large language models (LLMs) have opened the door to reliably mark and provide meaningful feedback on open-response tasks, supporting effective retrieval practice and challenging students to think deeply.

In this talk, we'll share our approach to using LLMs to automatically mark prose in Sparx Science, including: fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and everything in between.

events.title: From Gut Feelings to Data: Quantifying Proctor Judgment in High-Stakes Exams
events.speaker: Will Belzak
events.speakerBio: Will is a Senior Assessment Scientist leading test security and psychometric research at Duolingo. He holds a PhD in Quantitative Psychology from UNC - Chapel HIll and currently lives in Pittsburgh with his wife and son.
events.description: As high-stakes exams move online, ensuring their integrity poses both technical and human challenges. This talk focuses on quantifying the quality of human judgment in proctoring—a critical but often overlooked aspect of test security. Like other professionals, proctors make high-stakes decisions under uncertainty, with judgments influenced by lapses in attention, inconsistent training, and individual biases. We introduce the Professional Calibration Tool (PCT), a psychometric system that both measures and increases decision accuracy and reliability by embedding stealth assessments—pre-adjudicated cases—into live workflows and delivering real-time feedback based on expert and peer consensus.

events.title: Discretion in the Loop: Human Expertise in Algorithm-Assisted College Advising
events.speaker: Kara Schechtman
events.speakerBio: Kara Schechtman is a PhD student in Computer Science at Princeton University, where she researches the ethics of algorithmic decision making. Her current work explores how causal inference methods can inform the evaluation of algorithmic decision aids for both effectiveness and fairness. Prior to her doctoral studies, Kara received an MS in Symbolic Systems from Stanford University as a Knight-Hennessy Scholar and led the data quality team of The COVID Tracking Project at The Atlantic, which produced a widely used dataset on United States COVID-19 incidence and mortality.
events.description:
In higher education, many institutions use algorithmic alerts to flag at-risk students and deliver advising at scale. While much research has focused on the accuracy of algorithmic alert systems, less is known about how advisors translate risk predictions into effective interventions.

In this talk, Kara will present evidence that advisors' *discretionary* judgments in acting on predictions may be key to these tools' success, using rich quantitative and qualitative data from a randomized controlled trial of an algorithm-assisted advising program at Georgia State University, the Monitoring Advisor Analytics to Promote Success (MAAPS) experiment. We present a framework combining causal modeling, statistical testing, and qualitative analysis to study one kind of discretionary judgment by advisors, the incorporation of non-algorithmic context to "expertly" target interventions to students, in the MAAPS experiment.

The results suggest advisors incorporate diverse non-algorithmic information into their intervention decisions, with an estimated 2 in 3 interventions in the MAAPS experiment that may have been "expertly targeted" by advisors. The findings shed light on the role of advisor expertise in a real-world algorithm-assisted advising program and underscore the importance of accounting for human discretion in the design, evaluation, and implementation of algorithmic decision systems in education.

This talk is based on joint work with Sofiia Druchyna, Benjamin Brandon, Jenise Stafford, Hannah Li, and Lydia Liu.

events.title: The need for multidisciplinary education research: How racism shapes education
events.speaker: Jade Mai Cock
events.speakerBio:
I recently graduated with a PhD in Computer Science, where the main topic was to understand how students conduct inquiry on open-ended learning environments. 
As a fierce advocate for social justice, I, of course, also had to integrate that aspect into my thesis. And so, I dedicated a significant part of my PhD understanding how we could make our models fairer.

Beyond research, I try my best to make our communities more aware of the existing oppressive systemic dynamics, and try my bestest to make my local community better baby steps by baby steps. 

In doing so, together with brilliant women of colour, I co-founded [www.racism-search.be](http://www.racism-search.be/), a non profit that documents and democratises research about structural racism in Belgium. 

As these are quite heavy topics, you’ll probably find me skiing (when the mountains allow it), dancing, or making music to decompress!
events.description:
Racism can take many forms, some of them can be very obvious, others are more subtle.

Without a deep understanding of the different dynamics that can affect people of colour, and how these dynamics change based on context, history, geography, and other demographic attributes, it can be hard to understand how they can affect education, and specifically how they can affect the algorithms deployed in education.

In this talk, I will give an overview of the different types of racism, how they may interact with each other, and how that may translates in the context of educational data mining. Of course, we will go through an overview of how we can (hopefully) make EDM a fairer place by covering a subset of existing algorithmic mitigation techniques, as well as a framework to think about how racism may transpire in our pipelines.

events.title: Scaling Teacher Learning Through Automated Feedback: An Evaluation for K-12
events.speaker: Alyssa Van Camp
events.speakerBio: Alyssa Van Camp is Head of Research at TeachFX, where she leads research and development projects focused on AI powered classroom audio feedback for teacher professional learning.
events.description:
Automated feedback provides a scalable approach to supporting teacher reflection and improving instruction. However, there is limited evidence on how these technologies impact multiple dimensions of teacher and student outcomes in authentic school settings. This mixed-methods study evaluated a 4-5 week pilot of providing professional learning and automated feedback to K-12 teachers. We examined its impact on teacher well-being, teaching practice, classroom talk, and student engagement.

Findings indicate that automated feedback is associated with reductions in teacher burnout, improvements in self-efficacy, and increased perceptions of student engagement. Impacts on teaching practices were mixed: teachers increased their use of specific praise and wait time but decreased their use of open-ended questions and pressing students for reasoning. These findings suggest the potential of automated feedback to support teacher well-being and inform instructional changes, while highlighting areas for further research on sustaining and broadening practice improvements.

events.title: Transforming Learning Experiences with Personalized Data Intelligence in iTELL
events.speaker: Langdon Holmes
events.speakerBio: Langdon Holmes is a PhD candidate at Vanderbilt University specializing in educational technology and natural language processing. His research focuses on the role of prediction in second language acquisition alongside his work developing, refining, and deploying AI-enhanced learning platforms. As a core researcher on the iTELL team, Langdon develops analytics systems that power personalized learning experiences.
events.description: The digital transformation of education has generated unprecedented volumes of learning data, yet most reading platforms remain static, one-size-fits-all experiences. This session explores how modern analytics and AI are revolutionizing reading through personalized learning environments that adapt to individual learners. Drawing from real-world implementation in the iTELL platform, I'll demonstrate how hierarchical Bayesian modeling creates dynamic scoring thresholds, how semantic analysis targets knowledge gaps through strategic remediation, and how gamification elements driven by performance analytics support engagement. Attendees will learn about adaptive learning technologies that combine reading behavior telemetry, content analysis, and performance data to create personalized educational experiences.

events.title: AI-driven and Closed-loop Human Tutor Training and Real-life Assessment
events.speaker: Danielle R. Thomas
events.speakerBio: Danielle R. Thomas is a Systems Scientist at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. She serves as the Research Lead for PLUS (Personalized Learning Squared) and the Director of Research to Practice at the National Tutoring Observatory. As a former middle school math teacher, she focuses on "closing the loop" between human instruction and student learning.
events.description:
There exists a critical disconnect between human tutor professional development and actual student learning. In this talk, I will present a novel, AI-driven system designed to "close the loop" between human tutor training, real-world pedagogical actions, and student learning outcomes.

I will discuss a "learning by doing" approach where tutors practice specific competencies via AI-enhanced scenarios. Moving beyond simple training metrics, I will demonstrate how we utilize Large Language Models (Gemini-2.5-pro) to analyze transcripts of authentic, real-life tutoring sessions. We will explore the data science techniques used to validate this pipeline—specifically, how we measure the transfer of skills from tutor training to practice and how we establish the internal validity linking those specific "tutor moves" to demonstrable gains in student learning. This session will offer a roadmap for using AI to rigorously validate the impact of workforce training on the ultimate goal: student success.

events.title: Towards Impact-Oriented Benchmarks for AI Tutors
events.speaker: Kirk Vanacore
events.speakerBio: Kirk Vanacore is an Assistant Research Professor in the Bowers College of Computing and Information Science at Cornell University and the Research Director of the National Tutoring Observatory. He applies statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence to investigate causal mechanisms of learning in environments that blend human and AI instruction. His recent work focuses on leveraging AI to analyze tutoring-session data at scale while integrating rigorous quasi-experimental methods to identify what makes tutoring effective. He also studies how gamification, generative AI feedback, and tutoring interventions influence student persistence and self-regulated learning.
events.description:
Recent educational AI benchmarks show that while many foundation models perform well on broad pedagogical knowledge tests, their performance drops on harder tutoring tasks such as diagnosing specific algebra misconceptions, integrating visual student work, and using strong pedagogical moves like Socratic scaffolding. Even so, strong performance on difficult tutoring tasks is not the same as evidence of instructional impact. This talk takes up a central question for AI tutor benchmarking: does an AI tutor make decisions that improve learning? It introduces the idea of causal benchmarks for AI tutoring, a framework for evaluating tutor behavior based on its relationship to student outcomes.

The proposed framework has four parts: identifying which tutoring sessions are effective, locating the critical moments where tutor choices matter most, determining which tutor moves are most productive at those moments, and evaluating whether AI tutors choose those moves. This talk will present a causal analysis of session effect estimation, preliminary analyses of identifying critical moments, and a large-scale annotation effort focused on tutor moves. Together, these components suggest a path toward benchmarks that complement existing evaluation approaches by shifting attention from surface quality to instructional effectiveness. The talk will also highlight the methodological and practical challenges of building such benchmarks and discuss how this agenda could support more rigorous evaluation of future AI tutoring systems.
events.contentHtml:
Kirk opened by motivating the need for AI tutor benchmarks. Despite caution from experts like the Brookings Institution, these tools are already being used at scale, with students turning to off-the-shelf models for instruction.

He introduced the idea of benchmarks more generally, starting with ImageNet and MNIST, used for image classification and handwritten digit recognition. He then pointed to more language-oriented ones like SQuAD and MMLU, which are used to evaluate LLMs on answer extraction and multiple-choice questions.

Kirk then presented two tutoring conversations and asked participants to rate them and explain their reasoning. The scores ranged widely — from 2/10 to 7/10 for the same conversation.

Critiquing benchmarks.ai-for-education.org, he walked through some of the benchmarks available. The visual maths benchmark, for example, measures how well models handle visual mathematical problems, such as counting the number of bricks missing from a wall. But Kirk argued that these don't get at the quality of instruction. Task-based benchmarks come closer: MathDial pairs expert teachers with LLM-simulated students, and MathTutorBench provides two tasks covering verifiable skills and open-ended tutoring moves.

Kirk argued that existing benchmarks rest on three core assumptions which are not necessarily true:

  1. Content and pedagogical knowledge are good proxies for tutor quality.
  2. Tutoring quality is about increasing good behaviours and minimising bad ones — yet sometimes it is right to reveal an answer, for instance to a novice.
  3. Good tutoring can be reliably identified by expert educators.

This last point sounds a bit controversial, but Kirk pointing both to the disagreement among us on this very call and to studies showing that observed student outcomes are not closely tied to these expert evaluations.

He then offered a strawman for impact-oriented benchmarks, arguing that we are currently missing three things:

  1. Evaluations of when a tutoring response matters most.
  2. Evaluations of how students respond to an AI tutor.
  3. Evaluation of learning gains.

He proposed implementing this in four steps:

  1. Identify effective vs ineffective sessions
  2. Estimate effectiveness turn-by-turn
  3. Locate the critical moments
  4. Evaluate tutor behaviour at those moments

This then led to the following research challenges:

  1. Determining session-level effectiveness
  2. Models for predicting student outcomes from dialogue
  3. Simulations of plausible student responses

There was a great question about evaluating this approach against human tutor transcripts. Kirk suggested that AI tutors may need different strategies altogether, since students interact with them differently than they do with human tutors.

I don't think we've ever had so much engagement with a talk, a hot topic paired with a genuinely thoughtful analysis.

If you're interested in this space, check out the National Tutoring Observatory's "Trace the Ace" competition: Competition – Trace the Ace.
